lessons.title: Live in the Hour You Have
lessons.hook: Where was your mind during your last meal: on the food, or on tomorrow's to-do list?
lessons.idea:
The past is finished and the future hasn't arrived yet. The only moment you can actually act in is this one.

Worry about next month and regret about last year both pull attention away from the one place you can do something. Coming back to the present isn't ignoring the future. It's how you build it.
lessons.example:
Sam has a big exam in two weeks. Every evening he thinks about the whole syllabus at once and ends up too overwhelmed to start.

He changes the question to: "What can I learn in the next 45 minutes?" The overwhelm fades. By exam day he has covered more than he did in the whole month before.

quiz.question: Sam felt overwhelmed by a big exam. What shift helped him most?
options: Thinking about the entire syllabus every night
Focusing on what he could do in the next 45 minutes
quiz.explanation: Shrinking the focus to the next small block of time turned a frightening mountain into a step he could actually take.

lessons.action:
Set a timer for 10 minutes and do one task with your full attention.

Each time your mind drifts to the past or the future, notice it without judging yourself, and gently come back.

lessons.title: Do One Thing Completely
lessons.hook: How many "open tabs" are running in your head right now?
lessons.idea:
Splitting your attention feels productive, but it usually makes each task slower and sloppier.

Doing one thing at a time, and doing it as if it matters, gives you better work and a quieter mind. Even small tasks done fully can become a source of steadiness.
lessons.example:
Ana, a nurse, used to write notes while answering questions and planning her next visit all at once. Her shifts felt frantic.

She tried finishing each small task before starting the next: wash hands fully, write the note fully, then move on. Her shifts felt calmer, and she had to correct far fewer notes at the end of the day.

quiz.question: Why does doing one thing at a time help, according to this lesson?
options: It gives better results and a calmer mind
It lets you avoid hard tasks
It means you never have to plan
It only matters for big, important tasks
quiz.explanation: Full attention improves the work itself and lowers the background noise in your head, even for small tasks.

lessons.action:
Choose one routine task today, like washing the dishes, answering an email or taking a short walk.

Give it your complete attention from start to finish.

lessons.title: Let Limited Time Sharpen Your Choices
lessons.hook: Imagine counting how many more summers you'll get. Does the number make today feel a little more valuable?
lessons.idea:
Remembering that your time is limited isn't meant to be gloomy. It works like a filter.

It helps you drop petty grudges, busywork and endless "someday" plans, and spend your hours on what actually matters to you.
lessons.example:
Jordan kept putting off calling an old friend "until things calm down." Months went by.

When a relative fell suddenly ill, Jordan realised "later" isn't guaranteed. They called the friend that same evening. Now the two of them talk every month, and Jordan says it's one of the best parts of their week.

quiz.question: How does remembering that time is limited help, according to this lesson?
options: It makes you anxious, so you work harder
It helps you let go of small things and act on what matters
It shows that planning is pointless
It encourages you to rush through everything
quiz.explanation: It's a filter, not a source of fear. It makes it easier to see what deserves your time.

lessons.action:
Name one meaningful thing you've been putting off "until later."

Take the first small step today, even a two-minute version of it.
